Safely
SAYF-lee
adv.
From safe, through Old French sauf, from Latin salvus, whole, unhurt — the same root as salvation. Webster 1828: in a safe manner; without incurring danger or injury; without escape or loss. In Scripture safety is always located in a Person, never in circumstances.

Biblical Definition

Safely in Scripture describes the condition of those God keeps, and the texts are careful to name the cause. Wisdom’s promise closes the first chapter of Proverbs: whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil (Proverbs 1:33) — and the whole chapter has been an account of the young man refusing to hearken. The psalmist ties safety to sleep, which is the body’s daily confession of dependence: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). The word only is the doctrine. God led Israel through the sea and made his own people to go forth like sheep, and guided them in the wilderness like a flock. And he led them on safely, so that they feared not: but the sea overwhelmed their enemies (Psalm 78:52-53). The prophets promise it of the restored people: they shall dwell safely, and none shall make them afraid. And the New Testament transposes the whole idea into a Person: Paul, awaiting execution, says I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day — safety not of the body, which was about to be killed, but of the deposit.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SAFELY as in a safe manner, without incurring danger or injury, and without escape or loss; and SAFE as free from danger, unhurt, whole. The Latin salvus underlies both safe and salvation.

expand to see more

SAFELY, adv. — In a safe manner; without incurring danger or hazard of injury.

Without escape; without loss; as, the prisoner was safely kept.

SAFE, a. — Free from danger of any kind; unhurt; not lost; whole.

From Latin salvus, whole, sound, unhurt — the root of salvation, salve, and salutary.

That the English words for safety and for salvation share a root is not accidental: to be saved in Scripture is first of all to be made whole and kept.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 1:33 — "But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil."

Psalm 4:8 — "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety."

Psalm 78:53 — "And he led them on safely, so that they feared not: but the sea overwhelmed their enemies."

Proverbs 18:10 — "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe."

2 Timothy 1:12 — "For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day."

Modern Corruption

Safety has become the highest good of the age and the justification for nearly anything, while Scripture treats it as a gift located in God and freely spends the bodies of the saints.

expand to see more

The elevation of safety into a supreme value produces a religion that cannot account for the New Testament. Christ sent the twelve out as sheep in the midst of wolves and told them plainly they would be delivered up to councils and scourged; He said whoever would save his life should lose it. Paul lists his shipwrecks, stonings, and perils among his credentials. Hebrews 11 divides into those who by faith escaped the edge of the sword and those who by faith were sawn asunder, and both lists are commendations. A church that will not risk anything has quietly adopted a value the apostles did not hold, and it will find itself unable to obey ordinary commands about hospitality, evangelism, and care of the sick.

This is not a call to recklessness, which Scripture also condemns; the prudent man foreseeth the evil and hideth himself, and Paul was let down over a wall in a basket. The point is where safety is located. Proverbs 18:10 gives it exactly: the name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe — a tower, not a wall around his circumstances, and safety consisting in being inside it. Psalm 4:8 makes God the sole author, thou, LORD, only. And 2 Timothy 1:12 shows what is actually guaranteed: Paul in a Roman prison, certain of execution, persuaded that the deposit he had committed to Christ was safe against that day. His body was not safe. Nothing that mattered was in danger.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew betach (H983), security, confidence, safely, from batach, to trust; yasha (H3467), to save or deliver; Latin salvus behind the English.

expand to see more

Hebrew betach (H983) — security, safety, confidently; from batach, to trust or lean on.

Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to be confident; the root, so that to dwell safely is to dwell trustingly.

Hebrew yasha (H3467) — to save, deliver, give victory; the root of Joshua and of Jesus.

Hebrew migdal oz — a strong tower; the name of the LORD is a strong tower (Proverbs 18:10).

Greek paratheke (G3866) — a deposit committed to another’s keeping; that which I have committed unto him (2 Timothy 1:12).

Usage

"Whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely (Proverbs 1:33) — safety promised to the one who listens."

"Thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8) — the word only carries the doctrine."

"Able to keep that which I have committed unto him (2 Timothy 1:12) — a condemned man’s definition of safe."
